tagline: A winding ridge road connects forests and meadows with bay and ocean views.
intro: Skyline Boulevard follows the Santa Cruz Mountains’ ridge on a mostly two-lane highway, with a winding roadway used by motorists and cyclists. Its elevation brings both San Francisco Bay and the Pacific Ocean into view. Caltrans has designated the stretch ending at SR 92 as a scenic highway, recognizing a landscape without visual intrusions. Open-space preserves border the road, with trails beginning at roadside parking areas. Sports cars and motorcycles gather near the SR 84 intersection, particularly on weekends.

Skyline was originally State Route 5. The 1964 highway renumbering changed it to Route 35 to avoid confusion with Interstate 5. The adjoining landscape changed too: at Russian Ridge, dairy land passed to owners planning subdivisions before the open-space district began acquiring it in 1978. The ridgetop road ends at SR 92 because the mountain land farther north is a protected watershed owned by the San Francisco Water Department.

Starting at SR 92 and heading south, the ridge drive passes Kings Mountain and Skeggs Point before reaching Sky Londa at SR 84. Continue past Windy Hill and Russian Ridge toward Long Ridge near the county line. Long Ridge itself rises to about 2,600 feet on private property; the open-space preserve takes its name from that ridge.

moments.title: Sky Londa
moments.text: Sky Londa sits where Skyline Boulevard meets La Honda Road, at an elevation of 1,520 feet. The community’s name appears as Sky L’onda on maps dating to 1909; the U.S. Board of Geographic Names approves the spelling Sky Londa. Many of its redwood-log homes began in the early 1930s, when a developer subdivided tracts and established a water supply for the community. Their logs came from unused railroad-tie stock sawn at a mill that operated at the intersection until the Depression. Motorcycle and bicycle riders frequent the crossroads, especially on spring and summer weekends.

moments.title: Windy Hill
moments.text: Windy Hill’s open, grassy slopes rise above Portola Valley to a 1,905-foot summit. From Skyline Boulevard, the summit is a half-mile walk on a moderate grade. In clear weather, the view crosses Stanford University toward San Francisco Bay, Mount Tamalpais and Mount Diablo; San Francisco and the Pacific Ocean are also visible. The preserve also contains forested trails through oak, fir, buckeye, bay laurel and madrone, so its open summit represents only part of the landscape. Spring Ridge Trail connects Portola Valley with Skyline Boulevard through the grassy portion, while Hamms Gulch and other southern trails enter forest.
moments.notice: Open grassland contrasts with the preserve’s oak, fir and bay laurel woods.

moments.title: Russian Ridge Open Space Preserve
moments.text: Russian Ridge combines dense forest with open meadows, rising to Borel Hill at 2,572 feet. From the hill, views reach east across San Francisco Bay and west to the Pacific. The name recalls Mr. Paskey, a Russian immigrant who leased a dairy farm here from James Rolph Jr., San Francisco’s mayor and later California’s governor. The Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District began acquiring land in 1978 from owners who planned subdivisions. Poppies and lupines dominate the meadows from spring into early summer. By late summer the hills turn gold, with cluster-lily, gumweed, mule’s ear and farewell to spring among the flowers.
moments.notice: Poppies and lupines dominate the meadows in spring and early summer.
